newsitem.title: USA: U.S. protests use of force by police in Serbia.
newsitem.headline: U.S. protests use of force by police in Serbia.

text.p: The United States protested to the Yugoslav government over the weekend about police use of force against opposition protesters, the State Department said on Monday.

Spokesman Nicholas Burns said charge d'affaires Richard Miles delivered the protest -- the first on this issue -- to Yugoslav Foreign Minister Milan Milutinovic over what Washington said was a violation of a pledge not to use force.

Serbia's ruling Socialists, refusing to accept opposition victories in local elections last November, have loosened the leash on riot police faced with daily demonstrations. Since Thursday, police have pummeled protesters in several cities and seriously injured seven people in an attack on demonstrators sitting on a highway outside the provincial city of Kragujevac.

"The Serbian government made a pledge a couple of months ago that it would not use force against the people who are demonstrating peacefully. It has now reneged on that pledge. It has violated it. It is using force," Burns said.
"It cannot hope to attract international support, certainly not from governments like the United States government, if it continues to use physical force, police force, against innocent civilians."

Burns termed the authorities' action "a systematic use of the police to intimidate" demonstrators. He said the U.S. protest called on Belgrade to cease the use of force and warned that Washington would hold it responsible for its actions, but he said later he did not believe the demarche contained any specific threats.

The United States is already witholding high-level visits and discouraging trade with Serbia in protest against the government's refusal to recognise victory by the Zajedno opposition group in most cities where it claims to have won.
Burns denounced a decision by a municipal court in Belgrade to overturn a ruling by the electoral commission awarding victory in the capital to Zajedno.

He called it "a step in the wrong direction, because it does not address the fact that the international community and a great majority of the Serbian people believe that the opposition Zajedno won the Belgrade city election freely and fairly ... and had that stolen from them."
